intro/hello: How do you spread one training run across thousands of G P Us?
intro/budget: Start with the bill. Training costs about six operations per parameter, per token.
intro/model: Take a seventy B model and fifteen trillion tokens, roughly the budget of Llama three, seventy B.
intro/total: Six, times seventy billion, times fifteen trillion: about six times ten to the twenty-four operations.
intro/gpu: An H one hundred manages about four hundred trillion of those per second, in practice.
intro/years: So a single G P U would take about five hundred years.
intro/mem: Memory is no kinder: this model's training state is over a trillion bytes.
intro/many: So big models train on thousands of G P Us at once. The question is how to split the work.
intro/moves: There are only a few moves. Copy the model and split the data. Stop keeping copies. Split the matrices. Split the layers.
intro/plan: Each one trades memory for communication. We start by counting where the memory goes.
memory/recap: Training with Adam, in mixed precision, keeps five numbers for every parameter.
memory/w: The weights, in sixteen-bit B F sixteen: two bytes.
memory/master: A thirty-two-bit master copy of the weights, four bytes, so tiny updates do not round away.
memory/adam: And Adam's two running averages, m and v, four bytes each.
memory/total: That is sixteen bytes per parameter, before a single activation is stored.
memory/big: For a seventy billion parameter model, that is one point one two terabytes: fourteen G P Us of eighty gigabytes each, just to hold it.
memory/share: Look at the split. Only two of the sixteen bytes are the weights the forward pass uses. Twelve are optimizer state.
memory/fp32: Mixed precision does not shrink this: pure thirty-two-bit Adam is also sixteen bytes. It saves compute and activations instead.
activations/need: Backprop needs every layer's inputs from the forward pass, so the forward pass has to keep them.
activations/grows: Those saved values are the activations, and they grow with the tokens each G P U processes.
activations/count: A G P T style block saves about thirty-four bytes, per token, per unit of model width.
activations/gpt3: For G P T three, one two-thousand-token sequence needs about eighty-two gigabytes: more than a whole G P U.
activations/forward: Here are eight layers. As the forward pass runs, each one fills up with saved activations.
activations/backward: The backward pass frees them, last layer first. The peak comes right at the turn.
activations/ckpt: Activation checkpointing keeps only each block's input, a thin sliver, and throws the rest away.
activations/redo: When the backward pass reaches a block, it reruns that block's forward pass, then backpropagates through it.
activations/peak: The peak drops from a hundred and thirty-six units to twenty-four.
activations/cost: The price is one extra forward pass: about a third more compute, for over ten times less memory.
data/copies: The simplest split is data parallelism. Put a full copy of the model on every G P U.
data/slice: Cut each batch into N slices, and give each G P U its own.
data/grad: Each G P U runs forward and backward on its slice, and gets its own gradient.
data/avg: Now average the gradients across G P Us, and hand every G P U the average.
data/same: Every copy takes the identical step, so the copies stay identical forever.
data/exact: Because the loss is an average over the batch, this is exactly the whole batch's gradient. The math does not change.
data/allreduce: The one new operation is called all reduce. Everyone contributes an array, and everyone gets back the sum.
data/size: Here the array is the whole gradient: fourteen gigabytes for a seven billion parameter model, every step.
ring/naive: The obvious all reduce sends every gradient to one G P U, which adds them up and sends the sum back.
ring/bottleneck: That G P U's link carries N minus one gradients in, and N minus one out. Add G P Us, and it only gets worse.
ring/ring: The ring all reduce keeps every link equally busy. Arrange the G P Us in a ring, and cut each gradient into N chunks.
ring/rs: First, reduce-scatter. In each step, every G P U passes one chunk to its neighbor, who adds it to its own.
ring/own: After N minus one steps, each G P U holds the complete sum of one chunk.
ring/ag: Then all-gather: pass the finished chunks around the ring for N minus one more steps, until everyone has all of them.
ring/cost: Every step moves one N-th of the gradient per G P U. In total, each sends two times N minus one, over N, times the gradient.
ring/flat: That climbs from one toward two, and stops. Doubling the G P Us barely changes the time. This is why data parallelism scales.
ring/latency: What does grow is the number of steps, each with a small fixed delay, so gradients travel in big buckets.
ring/halves: Remember the two halves, reduce-scatter and all-gather. Sharding is built from them.
overlap/hide: An all reduce only costs time if the G P Us sit waiting for it.
overlap/buckets: The backward pass produces gradients from the last layer to the first. PyTorch's D D P groups them into buckets.
overlap/overlap: Each bucket's all reduce starts as soon as its gradients are ready, while the backward pass carries on with earlier layers.
overlap/ratio: Will the network keep up? Sending takes about four bytes per parameter over the link speed. Computing takes six operations per parameter per token.
overlap/cancel: Divide one by the other, and the model size cancels. What is left is two F, over three T B.
overlap/tokens: T is the number of tokens each G P U handles per step. Over InfiniBand, it needs to be well above five thousand.
overlap/shrink: Cut the tokens per G P U, and compute shrinks, but the gradient to send does not. The waiting grows.
overlap/limit: And the global batch is N times T. Past a critical batch size, bigger batches stop helping, so you cannot just keep adding G P Us.
overlap/memory: Data parallelism has a second limit. Every G P U still holds all sixteen bytes per parameter.
zero/copies: With N data-parallel G P Us, there are N identical copies of everything, most of them needed only briefly.
zero/zero: Zero, the zero redundancy optimizer, from Microsoft in 2019, removes the copies in three stages.
zero/s1: Stage one shards the optimizer state. Each G P U keeps Adam's state for one N-th of the parameters, and updates only that slice.
zero/rs: Gradients are reduce-scattered, so each G P U gets the averaged gradient for exactly its slice. Then an all-gather shares the new weights.
zero/free: Reduce-scatter plus all-gather is an all reduce: the same traffic as before. And twelve of the sixteen bytes are now divided by N.
zero/s2: Stage two also drops the gradients a G P U does not own. Same traffic again.
zero/s3: Stage three shards the weights too. Each layer's weights are gathered just before it runs, and freed right after.
zero/cost3: That is one and a half times the traffic, but every byte of state lives on exactly one G P U.
zero/nums: The Zero paper's example: seven and a half billion parameters on sixty-four G P Us. A hundred and twenty gigabytes each drops to thirty-one, seventeen, and under two.
zero/fsdp: PyTorch's F S D P, fully sharded data parallel, is stage three, wrapped around each block.
zero/acts: Sharding does not touch the activations, and each layer must still fit on one G P U. For that, we split the model itself.
tensor/inside: Megatron L M, from Nvidia in 2019, splits the work inside each layer.
tensor/mlp: Take the transformer's M L P. X times W one, a gell you, then times W two.
tensor/cols: A matrix product can be split by columns. Each column of the output needs only the matching column of W one.
tensor/split1: So give each G P U a block of W one's columns. It computes its block of the hidden layer on its own.
tensor/gelu: The gell you works on each number separately, so it never needs the other block.
tensor/rows: Then split W two by rows, matching the blocks. Each G P U's product is a partial sum of the output.
tensor/ar: One all reduce adds the partial sums, and the result matches the one-G P U answer.
tensor/wrong: The order matters. Split W one by rows instead, and the gell you lands on partial sums, which is simply wrong without an extra all reduce.
tensor/attn: Attention splits the same way, by heads. So each block costs two all reduces forward, and two backward.
tensor/ratio: But these carry activations, and the next step waits for them. Over InfiniBand, they would take longer than the math.
tensor/nvlink: So tensor parallelism stays inside one server, usually eight ways, on N V link.
pipeline/depth: To reach beyond one server, split the model by depth. Cut the layers into p stages, one per G P U.
pipeline/send: Activations flow forward to the next stage, and gradients flow back. These are small messages between neighbors, fine across servers.
pipeline/idle: The problem is idleness. With one batch, only one G P U works at a time.
pipeline/micro: G pipe, from Google in 2018, splits each batch into m micro-batches, and streams them through.
pipeline/fill: Now different stages work on different micro-batches at the same time.
pipeline/bubble: What stays idle is the ramp at the start and the end of every step. That is the pipeline bubble.
pipeline/formula: Its share of the time is p minus one, over m plus p minus one.
pipeline/numbers: With four stages and one micro-batch, three quarters idle. With eight, about a quarter. With thirty-two, under nine percent.
pipeline/onef: One F one B, one forward then one backward, starts each backward pass as early as it can.
pipeline/memory: The bubble is the same, but a stage now holds at most p micro-batches' activations, instead of all m.
pipeline/later: Interleaved and zero-bubble schedules shrink it further, for more messages.
sequence/intro: Three more splits complete the toolbox.
sequence/seq: Sequence parallelism helps tensor parallelism. Layer norms and dropouts are copied across a tensor group, so split them by token instead.
sequence/free: The all reduce becomes a reduce-scatter and an all-gather: the same traffic, and those activations shrink for free.
sequence/ctx: Context parallelism is for very long sequences. Split one sequence's tokens across G P Us.
sequence/ringattn: Attention needs every key and value, so they travel around a ring in blocks, while each G P U works on its own queries. That is ring attention.
sequence/ep: And a mixture-of-experts model puts different experts on different G P Us, with an all-to-all sending each token to its expert. That is expert parallelism.
threed/compose: Each method splits something different, so they compose. Arrange the G P Us as a grid, one axis per method.
threed/tp: Tensor parallelism has the heaviest traffic, so it gets the fastest wire: the G P Us inside one server.
threed/pp: Pipeline stages span servers. They only talk to their neighbors, with small messages.
threed/dp: Data parallelism, with Zero or F S D P, wraps around the outside. Its gradients move once per step, hidden behind the backward pass.
threed/llama: Meta's Llama three, four oh five B trained on up to sixteen thousand H one hundreds: tensor eight, pipeline sixteen, data one hundred and twenty-eight.
threed/deepseek: DeepSeek V three went another way: no tensor parallelism at all, sixteen pipeline stages, sixty-four-way expert parallelism, and Zero stage one.
threed/mfu: The score for all this engineering is model flops utilization: the share of peak arithmetic that goes into the model itself.
threed/forty: Every bubble, exposed all reduce and recomputed forward pass lowers it. Forty percent, at this scale, is doing well.
outro/mem: Training stores sixteen bytes per parameter, plus activations that grow with the tokens on each G P U.
outro/ckpt: Checkpointing trades a third more compute for most of the activation memory.
outro/dp: Data parallelism copies the model and averages gradients, with a ring all reduce whose cost barely grows with the G P Us.
outro/zero: Zero and F S D P stop keeping copies, using reduce-scatter and all-gather.
outro/tp: Tensor parallelism splits each layer by columns, then rows, and lives inside a server.
outro/pp: Pipeline parallelism splits the layers, and micro-batches shrink the bubble.
outro/wire: Underneath all of it is one rule: the heavier and less hideable the traffic, the faster the wire it gets.
outro/bye: Memory decides what must be split. Bandwidth decides where each split can live.
